title: Adobo pandesal
intro: Warm pandesal toasted in butter and stuffed with crisp adobo flakes. Salty, crunchy and soft at once, for breakfast or a packed snack.

steps.text: If using shredded leftover adobo, fry it in a dry pan with the adobo sauce over medium heat, stirring, until the sauce is absorbed and the meat is browned and crisp.
Split the pandesal without cutting all the way through. Spread the cut sides with butter.
Toast the pandesal cut side down in a pan over medium heat until golden.
Fill each roll with adobo flakes and a slice of tomato if using. Serve warm.

tips: A little mayonnaise or a fried egg in the roll turns this into a full breakfast.

title: Adobong pusit
intro: Small squid simmered briefly in vinegar, soy sauce and their own ink with garlic, onion and tomato. The sauce turns black, glossy and briny, and the squid stays tender.

steps.text: Clean the squid: pull the head away from the body, cut the tentacles just below the eyes and discard the eyes and beak. Pull out the clear quill. Set the silvery ink sacs aside in a small bowl.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and saute the garlic, onion and tomatoes until the tomatoes are soft.
Add the vinegar, soy sauce, water, sugar and pepper and bring to a boil without stirring.
Add the squid, then squeeze the ink from the sacs into the pan. Simmer just until the squid turns opaque.
Add the chili if using, taste and adjust, and serve right away with rice.

tips: Overcooked squid turns rubbery: keep it to a few minutes, or go past 30 minutes of gentle simmering until it softens again.

title: Adobong pusit sa gata
intro: Squid rings cooked in a vinegar and coconut milk sauce with ginger and chilies. Creamy, tangy and spicy, with tender squid.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and saute the garlic, onion and ginger until soft.
Add the vinegar and soy sauce and let them boil without stirring.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer uncovered, stirring now and then, until thickened.
Add the squid and simmer just until opaque.
Add the chilies and pepper, season with salt and serve with rice.

tips: Add the squid last and pull the pan off the heat as soon as it turns opaque so it stays tender.

title: Adobong hipon
intro: Shell-on shrimp cooked quickly in garlic, soy sauce and vinegar until the sauce reduces into a sticky, savory glaze. Ready in minutes.

steps.text: Trim the shrimp antennae and legs with scissors. Cut along the back of the shell and remove the vein.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat and fry the garlic until golden. Scoop out half for topping.
Add the shrimp and cook, tossing, until they start to turn pink.
Add the soy sauce, vinegar, water, sugar and pepper. Let it bubble for a minute without stirring, then toss and cook until the shrimp are cooked through and the sauce is reduced.
Top with the reserved garlic and serve with rice.

tips: The heads hold most of the flavor: press them with a spoon in the pan so their juices go into the sauce.

title: Adobong tahong
intro: Mussels steamed open in a garlicky soy and vinegar sauce with ginger. The mussel juices make the sauce briny and good over rice.

steps.text: Scrub the mussels, pull off the beards and discard any that are cracked or stay open when tapped.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat and saute the garlic, ginger and onion until soft.
Add the soy sauce, vinegar, water and pepper and bring to a boil without stirring.
Add the mussels, cover and cook, shaking the pot now and then, until the shells open.
Discard any mussels that stay closed. Scatter the green onions on top and serve with the sauce.

tips: Cook mussels the day you buy them and keep them in the fridge under a damp cloth until then, never in water.

title: Adobong pugita
intro: Octopus simmered until tender, then cut up and cooked in a garlicky soy and vinegar sauce. Meaty and slightly chewy with a glossy, savory sauce.

steps.text: Rub the octopus all over with the salt to remove the slime, then rinse well.
Put the octopus and bay leaves in a pot, add water to cover and simmer covered until a knife slides easily into the thickest part.
Drain, saving 1 cup of the cooking liquid. Cut the octopus into bite-size pieces.
Heat the oil in a pan and saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the octopus, soy sauce, reserved liquid and pepper. Bring to a boil, pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Simmer uncovered until the sauce is reduced and glossy. Add the chilies if using and serve with rice.

tips: Frozen octopus is often more tender than fresh because freezing breaks down the fibers; thaw it overnight in the fridge.

title: Adobong bangus
intro: Milkfish steaks fried until golden, then simmered in a garlicky soy and vinegar sauce. The fish stays flaky and the sauce is sharp and savory.

steps.text: Pat the fish dry and rub with the salt.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat and fry the fish until golden on both sides. Set aside.
Pour off all but 1 tablespoon of oil and fry the garlic until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce, water, bay leaves, peppercorns and sugar. Bring to a boil, add the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Return the fish and simmer, spooning the sauce over it, until the sauce has slightly reduced. Turn the fish only once so it does not break.
Serve with rice and the sauce spooned over.

tips: Boneless bangus works well here: cut the butterflied fish into four pieces and fry skin side first.

title: Adobong itlog ng pugo
intro: Boiled quail eggs simmered in a sweet-salty adobo sauce until glazed and brown. Bite-size, good with rice or as pulutan.

steps.text: Put the quail eggs in a pot of cold water, bring to a boil and boil. Drain, cover with cold water and peel.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and fry the garlic until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar, bay leaf and pepper and bring to a boil. Add the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Add the eggs and simmer, rolling them around, until the sauce is syrupy and the eggs are evenly browned.
Serve warm with rice.

tips: Roll the boiled eggs on the counter under your palm to crack the shell all over; it then peels off in one go. Canned quail eggs, drained, save all the peeling.

title: Adobong itlog
intro: Hard-boiled eggs fried until blistered, then simmered in garlicky adobo sauce until brown and glossy. A cheap, quick ulam when there is no meat in the fridge.

steps.text: Put the eggs in a pot of cold water, bring to a boil and cook. Cool in cold water, peel and make a few shallow slits in each.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat. Fry the eggs, rolling them, until the whites are blistered and golden. Use a lid as a shield since they can pop.
Remove the eggs and saute the garlic and onion in the same oil until soft.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar, bay leaves and peppercorns. Bring to a boil, add the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Return the eggs and simmer, turning them now and then, until the sauce is thick.
Halve the eggs and serve with the sauce over rice.

tips: Fried tofu cubes or fried potatoes can go in with the eggs to make it more filling.

title: Adobong tokwa
intro: Firm tofu fried until golden and crisp, then simmered briefly in garlicky soy and vinegar sauce so it soaks up the flavor. A meatless adobo that still tastes rich.

steps.text: Wrap the tofu in a clean towel and press it under a heavy pan to drain, then cut into cubes.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium-high heat and fry the tofu, turning, until golden and crisp on all sides. Drain on paper towels.
Pour off all but 1 tablespoon of oil. Saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar, bay leaves and pepper and bring to a boil. Add the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Add the tofu and simmer, tossing gently, until most of the sauce is absorbed.
Top with green onions and serve with rice.

tips: Pressing the tofu matters: drier tofu fries crisper and drinks up more sauce.

title: Adobong kabute
intro: Mushrooms seared until browned, then tossed in a garlicky soy and vinegar sauce. Meaty, savory and quick enough for a weeknight.

items.name: fresh mushrooms
items.note: button or shiitake, sliced or torn

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pan over high heat. Add the mushrooms in one layer and cook without stirring until browned underneath, then stir and cook until their liquid has evaporated.
Push the mushrooms aside and saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar, bay leaf and pepper, then the vinegar. Let it bubble without stirring.
Toss everything together and simmer until the sauce is glossy and coats the mushrooms.
Serve hot with rice.

tips: Do not crowd the pan or the mushrooms will steam instead of browning; cook them in two batches if needed.

title: Adobong kangkong
intro: Water spinach stir-fried with lots of garlic in a quick soy and vinegar sauce, with crunchy stems and soft leaves. A fast, cheap vegetable dish for rice.

steps.text: Wash the kangkong, separate the stems from the leaves and cut the stems into 2-inch pieces. Discard the tough bottom ends.
Heat the oil in a wok over medium heat and fry the garlic until golden. Scoop out half for topping.
Add the onion and the stems and stir-fry over high heat.
Add the soy sauce, vinegar, water, sugar and pepper and let it bubble without stirring.
Add the leaves and toss just until wilted.
Top with the reserved garlic and serve right away.

tips: Kangkong goes limp and dark fast, so cook it right before eating.

title: Adobong sitaw
intro: Long beans cooked with strips of pork belly in a savory adobo sauce until just tender. The pork fat flavors the beans, which stay bright and slightly crisp.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and fry the pork until browned and some fat has rendered.
Add the garlic and onion and saute until soft.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar and pepper. Cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Pour in the vinegar and let it boil without stirring.
Add the sitaw, cover and cook until tender but still bright green.
Uncover and toss until the sauce is reduced. Taste, adjust and serve with rice.

tips: For a meatless version, use fried tofu cubes instead of pork and add a little more oil.

title: Adobong talong
intro: Eggplant fried until soft and browned, then tossed in a garlicky soy and vinegar sauce that it soaks right up. Silky, savory and a little sweet.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat and fry the eggplant in batches until browned and soft. Drain on paper towels.
Pour off all but 1 tablespoon of oil. Saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar and pepper, then the vinegar, and let it boil without stirring.
Return the eggplant and toss gently until it is coated and the sauce is slightly reduced.
Serve warm with rice.

tips: Eggplant drinks oil: fry it in a hot pan and do not add more oil midway, it will release some back as it softens.

title: Adobong okra
intro: Okra seared in a hot pan until browned, then tossed in a quick garlicky adobo sauce. Tender-crisp and savory, without the sliminess of boiled okra.

steps.text: Make sure the okra is completely dry after washing.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over high heat. Lay the okra cut side down and sear without stirring until browned.
Push the okra aside and saute the garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar and pepper, then the vinegar. Let it bubble without stirring.
Toss and simmer until the okra is tender-crisp and coated in sauce.
Serve hot with rice.

tips: High heat and dry okra keep the slime down. Cook it just before eating.

title: Adobong ampalaya
intro: Thinly sliced bitter gourd cooked with ground pork in a garlicky adobo sauce. The salt and vinegar soften the bitterness while the pork adds richness.

steps.text: Toss the sliced ampalaya with the salt and let it sit, then squeeze out the liquid firmly and rinse once.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and brown the ground pork, breaking it up.
Add the garlic and onion and saute until soft.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar and pepper and simmer. Pour in the vinegar and let it boil without stirring.
Add the ampalaya, cover and cook until tender but still green.
Toss, taste and serve with rice.

tips: Squeeze the salted ampalaya hard: the more liquid comes out, the milder it tastes. Slicing it thin helps too.

title: Adobong puso ng saging
intro: Banana blossom sliced thin, squeezed of its bitter sap and simmered in a tangy adobo sauce. Tender and a little chewy, with a mild, artichoke-like flavor.

steps.text: Peel off the tough, dark outer bracts until you reach the pale inner heart. Slice it thinly crosswise.
Rub the slices with the salt, squeeze hard to press out the dark sap, then rinse and squeeze again. Repeat once more.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the banana blossom and stir-fry.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar and pepper, then the vinegar, and bring to a boil without stirring.
Cover and simmer until tender.
Uncover and cook until the sauce is reduced. Taste, adjust and serve with rice.

tips: Oil your knife and hands before slicing: the sap is sticky and stains. Slice straight into salted water so the pieces do not darken.

title: Adobong repolyo
intro: Cabbage stir-fried over high heat with garlic and a splash of soy sauce and vinegar until lightly charred and crisp-tender. A quick, budget-friendly side for rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wok over medium heat and fry the garlic until golden. Scoop out half for topping.
Add the onion and cook until soft.
Raise the heat to high, add the cabbage and stir-fry until the edges begin to char.
Add the soy sauce, vinegar, water, sugar and pepper. Let it bubble for a moment without stirring, then toss and cook until crisp-tender.
Top with the reserved garlic and serve.

tips: Add a few strips of fried pork belly or fried tofu to make it a full ulam.

title: Adobong labong
intro: Bamboo shoots boiled to remove their strong smell, then cooked with pork belly in a tangy adobo sauce. Crunchy, savory and slightly sour.

items.name: bamboo shoots (labong)
items.note: thinly sliced, fresh or drained from a jar

steps.text: Boil the bamboo shoots in plenty of water for 5 minutes, drain, and repeat twice with fresh water each time.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and fry the pork until browned and some fat has rendered.
Add the garlic and onion and saute until soft.
Add the bamboo shoots, soy sauce, water and pepper and simmer.
Pour in the vinegar and let it boil without stirring.
Simmer uncovered until most of the liquid is absorbed. Add the chili, toss and serve with rice.

tips: Fresh labong has a strong smell that the repeated boiling takes away; jarred shoots need only one boil.

title: Adobong sigarilyas
intro: Winged beans sliced and cooked with pork belly in a garlicky adobo sauce until bright green and crisp-tender. Crunchy and savory, a good way to use these frilly beans.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and fry the pork until browned and some fat has rendered.
Add the garlic and onion and saute until soft.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar and pepper. Cover and simmer.
Pour in the vinegar and let it boil without stirring.
Add the sigarilyas and cook, stirring, until bright green and tender-crisp.
Taste, adjust and serve with rice.

tips: Pick young, bright green pods that snap when bent; older ones turn stringy.

title: Adobong langka
intro: Young, unripe jackfruit boiled until tender, then browned and simmered in adobo sauce until glazed. Its shreddy texture makes a hearty meatless adobo.

items.name: young unripe jackfruit (langka)
items.note: peeled, cored and cut into chunks

steps.text: Boil the jackfruit in salted water until a fork goes in easily. Drain and pull the chunks apart a little with a fork.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and saute the garlic and onion until soft.
Add the jackfruit and fry until the edges are lightly browned.
Add the soy sauce, water, sugar, bay leaves and peppercorns and bring to a boil. Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Simmer uncovered, stirring now and then, until the sauce is reduced and the jackfruit is glazed.
Taste, adjust and serve with rice.

tips: Oil your knife and hands before cutting fresh jackfruit since the sap is very sticky. Canned young jackfruit in brine, drained and rinsed, skips the boiling.

title: Adobong mani
intro: Raw peanuts fried with their skins on alongside plenty of garlic, then tossed with salt and chili. Crunchy, salty and garlicky, a classic snack with drinks or on its own.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat and fry the garlic until golden. Scoop it out with a slotted spoon.
Lower the heat to medium-low, add the peanuts and fry, stirring constantly, until the skins darken slightly and the nuts smell toasty.
Scoop the peanuts onto paper towels and, while still hot, toss with the salt, fried garlic and chili flakes.
Let cool completely before serving; the peanuts crisp up as they cool.

tips: Pull the peanuts out a shade lighter than you want them since they keep cooking from the heat. Store in an airtight jar for up to two weeks.
